claim: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is a critical junction in both the indirect and hyperdirect pathways of the basal ganglia (BG).
source: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is a critical junction in both the indirect and hyperdirect pathways of the basal ganglia (BG).
evidence: This is established knowledge about STN anatomy and connectivity within the basal ganglia.

claim: The STN receives inputs from the external segment of the globus pallidum (GPe) and cortex.
source: It receives inputs from the external segment of the globus pallidum (GPe) and cortex and sends diffuse excitation to pallidal output nuclei of the BG.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about STN connectivity.

claim: The STN sends diffuse excitation to pallidal output nuclei of the BG.
source: It receives inputs from the external segment of the globus pallidum (GPe) and cortex and sends diffuse excitation to pallidal output nuclei of the BG.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about STN outputs.

claim: In humans and monkeys, lesions of the STN cause involuntary movements of contralateral body parts.
source: For example, in humans and monkeys, lesions of the STN cause involuntary movements of contralateral body parts (Martin, 1927; Martin and Alcock, 1934; Whittier and Mettler, 1949; Carpenter et al., 1950).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: In monkeys with experimentally induced parkinsonism, STN lesions and inactivation can reverse abnormal BG output activity.
source: In monkeys with experimentally induced parkinsonism, STN lesions and inactivation can reverse abnormal BG output activity and alleviate both akinesia and rigidity (Bergman et al., 1990; Bergman et al., 1994; Wichmann et al., 1994a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: In monkeys with experimentally induced parkinsonism, STN lesions and inactivation can alleviate both akinesia and rigidity.
source: In monkeys with experimentally induced parkinsonism, STN lesions and inactivation can reverse abnormal BG output activity and alleviate both akinesia and rigidity (Bergman et al., 1990; Bergman et al., 1994; Wichmann et al., 1994a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: In parkinsonian human patients, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the STN has become a common treatment option to alleviate movement abnormalities.
source: In parkinsonian human patients, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the STN has become a common treatment option to alleviate movement abnormalities (DeLong and Wichmann, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Motor symptoms associated with STN damage are often accompanied by emotional and cognitive deficits.
source: Recognizing that motor symptoms associated with STN damage are often accompanied by emotional and cognitive deficits, recent work has also begun to examine the roles of the STN in cognition.
evidence: This is stated as a recognized observation that motivates recent research.

claim: The STN has been shown to contribute to cued, goal-driven action inhibition.
source: For example, the STN has been shown to contribute to cued, goal-driven action inhibition (Baunez et al., 2001; Desbonnet et al., 2004; Witt et al., 2004; Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Frank et al., 2007; Isoda and Hikosaka, 2008; Schmidt et al., 2013; Pasquereau and Turner, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research studies.

claim: STN activity can be sensitive to task complexity and decision conflict.
source: STN activity can also be sensitive to task complexity and decision conflict, as measured in imaging studies and human patients undergoing DBS (Lehéricy et al., 2004; Aron et al., 2007; Fumagalli et al., 2011; Brittain et al., 2012; Zaghloul et al., 2012; Zavala et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Through its interaction with GPe, STN computes a normalization signal to calibrate how the available, alternative options are assessed.
source: (1) through its interaction with GPe, STN computes a normalization signal to calibrate how the available, alternative options are assessed (Bogacz and Gurney, 2007; Coulthard et al., 2012; Green et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from computational models cited in the text.

claim: In coordination with the medial prefrontal cortex, STN adjusts decision bounds to control impulsivity in responding.
source: (2) in coordination with the medial prefrontal cortex, STN adjusts decision bounds (i.e. thresholds on accumulated evidence that govern decision termination and commitment) to control impulsivity in responding (Frank, 2006; Cavanagh et al., 2011; Ratcliff and Frank, 2012; Zavala et al., 2014; Herz et al., 2016; Herz et al., 2017; Pote et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from computational models cited in the text.

claim: By maintaining the balance between the direct and indirect pathways of the BG, STN helps to implement a nonlinear computation that improves the efficacy with which the BG adjusts decision bounds.
source: (3) by maintaining the balance between the direct and indirect pathways of the BG, STN helps to implement a nonlinear computation that improves the efficacy with which the BG adjusts decision bounds (Lo and Wang, 2006; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from computational models cited in the text.

claim: 203 neurons were recorded while monkeys were performing a random-dot motion discrimination task.
source: We recorded 203 neurons while the monkeys were performing a random-dot motion discrimination task (n=115 and 88 for monkeys C and F, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data collected.

claim: 115 neurons were recorded from monkey C and 88 neurons from monkey F.
source: We recorded 203 neurons while the monkeys were performing a random-dot motion discrimination task (n=115 and 88 for monkeys C and F, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data collected.

claim: Both monkeys made more contralateral choices with increasing signed motion strength.
source: In general, both monkeys made more contralateral choices with increasing signed motion strength (positive for motion toward the contralateral target; negative for motion toward the ipsilateral target) and had lower RTs (i.e. faster responses) for higher absolute motion strength.
evidence: This is a description of behavioral performance data from the task.

claim: Both monkeys had lower RTs (i.e. faster responses) for higher absolute motion strength.
source: In general, both monkeys made more contralateral choices with increasing signed motion strength (positive for motion toward the contralateral target; negative for motion toward the ipsilateral target) and had lower RTs (i.e. faster responses) for higher absolute motion strength.
evidence: This is a description of behavioral performance data from the task.

claim: STN neurons showed diverse response profiles.
source: STN neurons showed diverse response profiles.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: STN neurons can become activated or suppressed, relative to pre-stimulus baseline, during motion viewing and around saccade onset.
source: When activity was averaged across all trial types, STN neurons can become activated or suppressed (warm vs. cool colors, respectively), relative to pre-stimulus baseline, during motion viewing and around saccade onset.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The timing of peak modulation in STN neurons spanned the entire motion-viewing period and extended beyond saccade generation.
source: The timing of peak modulation also spanned the entire motion-viewing period and extended beyond saccade generation, including a substantial fraction of neurons that also responded to target onset before the motion stimulus appeared.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A substantial fraction of STN neurons responded to target onset before the motion stimulus appeared.
source: The timing of peak modulation also spanned the entire motion-viewing period and extended beyond saccade generation, including a substantial fraction of neurons that also responded to target onset before the motion stimulus appeared.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The diverse spatiotemporal response profiles suggest that the STN as a whole may serve multiple functions in perceptual decision-making.
source: These diverse spatiotemporal response profiles suggest that the STN as a whole may serve multiple functions in perceptual decision-making.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed diversity in neural response patterns.

claim: A substantial fraction of STN neurons was sensitive to choice, motion coherence, and RT.
source: Across the population, a substantial fraction of neurons was sensitive to choice, motion coherence, and RT (Figure 2C–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the regression analysis results shown in the figures.

claim: Both contralateral and ipsilateral choice preferences were commonly observed in STN neurons.
source: For choice sensitivity (Figure 2C, first row), both contralateral and ipsilateral preferences were commonly observed.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The overall fraction of STN neurons showing choice sensitivity increased after motion onset and peaked at saccade onset.
source: The overall fraction of neurons showing choice sensitivity increased after motion onset and peaked at saccade onset (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The fraction of STN neurons showing reliable coherence sensitivity was higher around saccade onset.
source: The fraction of neurons showing reliable coherence sensitivity was also higher around saccade onset (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: STN neurons showing choice sensitivity were more likely to show coherence modulation during early motion viewing, especially for trials when the monkey chose the neuron's preferred choice.
source: Notably, neurons showing choice sensitivity were more likely to show coherence modulation during early motion viewing, especially for trials when the monkey chose the neuron's preferred choice (Figure 2E, purple).
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Coherence modulation emerged later for STN neurons that did not show choice sensitivity.
source: In contrast, coherence modulation emerged later for neurons that did not show choice sensitivity (Figure 2E, gray lines).
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The systematic interactions in modulation types suggest that the STN population does not simply reflect a random mix of selectivity for decision-related quantities.
source: These systematic interactions in modulation types suggest that the STN population does not simply reflect a random mix of selectivity for decision-related quantities.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed patterns in the data.

claim: There appear to exist STN subpopulations with distinct decision-related modulation patterns.
source: Instead, there appears to exist subpopulations with distinct decision-related modulation patterns, which we detail below.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed patterns in the data.

claim: Three subpopulations of neurons in the STN were identified with distinct activity patterns that conform to predictions of each of the three previously published sets of models.
source: Using two forms of cluster analysis, we identified three subpopulations of neurons in the STN with distinct activity patterns that conform to predictions of each of the three previously published sets of models.
evidence: This is a summary of the cluster analysis results.

claim: Bogacz and Gurney, 2007, posited that STN neurons, through their reciprocal connections with the external segment of GPe, pool and normalize evidence-related signals, leading to the prediction of choice and coherence-modulated activity during motion viewing.
source: Bogacz and Gurney, 2007, posited that STN neurons, through their reciprocal connections with the external segment of GPe, pool and normalize evidence-related signals, leading to the prediction of choice and coherence-modulated activity during motion viewing (Figure 3A, top; based on simulations using equations in their Appendix B).
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical prediction from a cited model.

claim: Ratcliff and Frank, 2012, posited that STN neurons, through their direct innervation by cortical regions, provide an early signal to suppress immature choices, leading to the prediction of a choice-independent signal that appears soon after motion onset and dissipates over time.
source: Ratcliff and Frank, 2012, posited that STN neurons, through their direct innervation by cortical regions, provide an early signal to suppress immature choices, leading to the prediction of a choice-independent signal that appears soon after motion onset and dissipates over time (Figure 3A, middle; based on their Figure 5).
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical prediction from a cited model.

claim: Wei et al., 2015, posited that the STN balances evidence-related signals in the GPe until near decision time, leading to the prediction of coherence-dependent ramping activity with no or weak choice selectivity.
source: Wei et al., 2015, posited that the STN balances evidence-related signals in the GPe until near decision time, leading to the prediction of coherence-dependent ramping activity with no or weak choice selectivity (Figure 3A, bottom; based on their Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical prediction from a cited model.

claim: The first cluster of STN neurons tends to show choice- and coherence-dependent activity that also ramps up during motion viewing.
source: Consistent with the design of this analysis, the first cluster tends to show choice- and coherence-dependent activity that also ramps up during motion viewing (Figure 3B, first row; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the cluster analysis results shown in the figures.

claim: The second cluster of STN neurons tends to show an early, sharper rise in activity during motion viewing and this activity gradually decreases toward saccade onset.
source: The second cluster tends to show an early, sharper rise in activity during motion viewing and this activity gradually decreases toward saccade onset (Figure 3B, second row).
evidence: This is a description of the cluster analysis results shown in the figures.

claim: The third cluster of STN neurons tends to show ramping activity during motion viewing with similar coherence modulation for both choices and a short burst of activity for one choice just before saccade onset.
source: The third cluster tends to show ramping activity during motion viewing with similar coherence modulation for both choices and a short burst of activity for one choice just before saccade onset (Figure 3B, third row; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the cluster analysis results shown in the figures.

claim: The first three clusters of STN neurons contained similar numbers of neurons.
source: The first three clusters contained similar numbers of neurons.
evidence: This is a description of the cluster analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When visualized using the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) technique, the STN neuron clusters did not form a single continuum but instead reflected separable features between clusters.
source: When visualized using the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) technique, these clusters did not form a single continuum but instead reflected separable features between clusters (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a description of the visualization results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The clustering did not simply force a uniform distribution with random-mixed selectivity into four groups.
source: In other words, the clustering did not simply force a uniform distribution with random-mixed selectivity into four groups.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the t-SNE visualization results.

claim: Random-seeded k-means clustering obtained almost identical clusters to model-seeded clustering.
source: For the second cluster analysis, we used random seeds without considering any of the model predictions and obtained almost identical clusters.
evidence: This is a summary of the second cluster analysis results.

claim: The silhouette plots favored the combination of using the 30D vector directly and correlation distance for clustering.
source: The silhouette plots favored the combination of using the 30D vector directly and correlation distance (Figure 4A, third row), which generated less variability across clusters and few small-magnitude negative silhouette scores (negative scores indicate that a member is closer to its neighboring cluster than its own cluster).
evidence: This is a description of the clustering quality assessment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Rand index was generally high (above 0.95 out of a max of 1) except for the combination of using the 30D vector and cosine distance.
source: The Rand index was generally high (above 0.95 out of a max of 1; blue box) except for the combination of using the 30D vector and cosine distance (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a description of the clustering stability assessment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Using the raw vector-correlation combination, an assumption of four clusters resulted in the highest average Rand index.
source: Finally, using the raw vector-correlation combination, an assumption of four clusters resulted in the highest average Rand index and assuming four to six clusters generally resulted in higher mean silhouette score and lower number of negative scores (Figure 4C; blue arrow).
evidence: This is a description of the clustering optimization results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The four clusters identified by random-seeded clustering closely matched those obtained using model predicted seeds, in terms of the average activity, the cluster sizes, and their locations in the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) space.
source: As shown in Figure 3D and E, the four clusters thus identified closely matched those obtained using model predicted seeds, in terms of the average activity, the cluster sizes, and their locations in the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) space.
evidence: This is a comparison of the two clustering approaches shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: There exist at least three STN subpopulations that each corresponds to the predictions of one of three previously published models.
source: Together these results suggest that, absent the ground truth on the number of subpopulations in STN, there exist at least three subpopulations that each corresponds to the predictions of one of three previously published models.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cluster analysis results.

claim: STN appears in principle to be able to support multiple decision-related functions.
source: As a consequence, STN appears in principle to be able to support multiple decision-related functions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the identification of multiple subpopulations with distinct functional properties.

claim: Electrical microstimulation was applied at identified STN sites during decision formation, lasting from motion onset to saccade onset.
source: Specifically, we applied a train of current pulses at identified STN sites during decision formation, lasting from motion onset to saccade onset.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: In the first example session, STN microstimulation caused a leftward horizontal shift (more contralateral choices) and slope reduction (more variable choices) in the psychometric curve.
source: In the first example session, STN microstimulation caused a leftward horizontal shift (more contralateral choices) and slope reduction (more variable choices) in the psychometric curve (Figure 5A, top), as well as a substantial flattening of RT curves (faster responses that depended less on motion coherence) for both choices (bottom).
evidence: This is a description of the microstimulation effects shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the first example session, STN microstimulation caused a substantial flattening of RT curves (faster responses that depended less on motion coherence) for both choices.
source: In the first example session, STN microstimulation caused a leftward horizontal shift (more contralateral choices) and slope reduction (more variable choices) in the psychometric curve (Figure 5A, top), as well as a substantial flattening of RT curves (faster responses that depended less on motion coherence) for both choices (bottom).
evidence: This is a description of the microstimulation effects shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the second example session, STN microstimulation induced a minor leftward shift in the psychometric curve and asymmetric changes in RT for the two choices.
source: In the second example session, STN microstimulation induced a minor leftward shift in the psychometric curve and asymmetric changes in RT for the two choices (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a description of the microstimulation effects shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the third example session, STN microstimulation did not change the psychometric curve but caused reductions in RT for both choices.
source: In the third example session, STN microstimulation did not change the psychometric curve but caused reductions in RT for both choices (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a description of the microstimulation effects shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Across 54 different STN sites, microstimulation caused variable choice biases and tended to reduce the dependence of choice on motion strength.
source: Across 54 different STN sites, microstimulation caused variable choice biases and tended to reduce the dependence of choice on motion strength.
evidence: This is a summary of the microstimulation effects across all sites.

claim: In 23 sessions, STN microstimulation induced a reliable choice bias.
source: In 23 sessions, microstimulation induced a reliable choice bias (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a summary of the microstimulation effects shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The induced bias was toward the contralateral or ipsilateral choice in 15 and 8 sessions, respectively.
source: The induced bias was toward the contralateral or ipsilateral choice in 15 and 8 sessions, respectively, and the median value for bias was not significantly different from zero (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.15).
evidence: This is a summary of the microstimulation effects on choice bias.

claim: The median value for bias was not significantly different from zero (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.15).
source: The induced bias was toward the contralateral or ipsilateral choice in 15 and 8 sessions, respectively, and the median value for bias was not significantly different from zero (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.15).
evidence: This is a statistical test result on the microstimulation effects.

claim: In 18 sessions, STN microstimulation induced a change in the slope of the psychometric curve.
source: In 18 sessions, microstimulation induced a change in the slope.
evidence: This is a summary of the microstimulation effects on psychometric slope.

claim: The slope of the psychometric curve was reduced in 15 sessions and the median value was negative (p=0.008).
source: The slope was reduced in 15 sessions and the median value was negative (p=0.008).
evidence: This is a summary of the microstimulation effects on psychometric slope with statistical test.

claim: STN microstimulation most consistently reduced the choice dependence on motion strength, caused session-specific choice biases, and had minimal effects on lapses.
source: Thus, based on fitting results using logistic functions, STN microstimulation most consistently reduced the choice dependence on motion strength, caused session-specific choice biases, and had minimal effects on lapses.
evidence: This is a summary of the logistic function fitting results.

claim: STN microstimulation tended to reduce RT.
source: Microstimulation also tended to reduce RT.
evidence: This is a summary of the microstimulation effects on RT.

claim: STN microstimulation caused changes in RT offsets in 25 sessions for contralateral choices (18 were reductions in RT, with a median change across all sessions of –36 ms; Wilcoxon signed-rank test for H0: median change = 0, p<0.0001).
source: Microstimulation caused changes in RT offsets in 25 sessions for contralateral choices (18 were reductions in RT, with a median change across all sessions of –36 ms; Wilcoxon signed-rank test for H0: median change = 0, p<0.0001) and 18 sessions for ipsilateral choices (15 reductions, mean change = –23 ms, p<0.0001; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a summary of the microstimulation effects on RT offsets with statistical tests.

claim: STN microstimulation caused changes in RT offsets in 18 sessions for ipsilateral choices (15 reductions, mean change = –23 ms, p<0.0001).
source: Microstimulation caused changes in RT offsets in 25 sessions for contralateral choices (18 were reductions in RT, with a median change across all sessions of –36 ms; Wilcoxon signed-rank test for H0: median change = 0, p<0.0001) and 18 sessions for ipsilateral choices (15 reductions, mean change = –23 ms, p<0.0001; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a summary of the microstimulation effects on RT offsets with statistical tests.

claim: STN microstimulation caused changes in RT slopes in 6 sessions for contralateral choices (5 were positive, implying a weaker coherence dependence; p<0.0001).
source: Microstimulation caused changes in RT slopes in 6 sessions for contralateral choices (5 were positive, implying a weaker coherence dependence; p<0.0001) and 4 sessions for ipsilateral choices (all 4 were positive; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a summary of the microstimulation effects on RT slopes with statistical tests.

claim: STN microstimulation caused changes in RT slopes in 4 sessions for ipsilateral choices (all 4 were positive).
source: Microstimulation caused changes in RT slopes in 6 sessions for contralateral choices (5 were positive, implying a weaker coherence dependence; p<0.0001) and 4 sessions for ipsilateral choices (all 4 were positive; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a summary of the microstimulation effects on RT slopes.

claim: STN microstimulation can induce choice-specific changes in RT, with overall tendencies to reduce both the coherence-independent component and the RT's dependence on coherence for the contralateral choice.
source: Thus, based on fitting results using linear functions, STN microstimulation can induce choice-specific changes in RT, with overall tendencies to reduce both the coherence-independent component and the RT's dependence on coherence for the contralateral choice.
evidence: This is a summary of the linear function fitting results.

claim: In 40 of 54 sessions, the Full model, which included microstimulation effects on any model parameters, outperformed the None model, which assumed that there was no microstimulation effect on any parameters.
source: We performed AIC-based model selection and found that, in 40 of 54 sessions, the Full model, which included microstimulation effects on any model parameters, outperformed the None model, which assumed that there was no microstimulation effect on any parameters (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a summary of the DDM model comparison results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In 40 of 54 sessions, STN microstimulation affected one or more computational components of the decision process.
source: This result implies that, in these sessions, STN microstimulation affected one or more computational components of the decision process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the DDM model comparison results.

claim: Consistent with model predictions from Bogacz and Gurney, 2007, microstimulation reduced the scale factor for evidence accumulation, k, in 14 sessions.
source: Consistent with model predictions from Bogacz and Gurney, 2007, microstimulation reduced the scale factor for evidence accumulation, k, in 14 sessions.
evidence: This is a summary of the DDM parameter fitting results related to a specific theoretical prediction.

claim: The reduction in the scale factor for evidence accumulation contributed to a decreased motion coherence dependence of choice and RT (Wilcoxon signed-rank test for H0: zero median effect, p=0.021).
source: This effect contributed to a decreased motion coherence dependence of choice and RT (Figure 6C, first histogram; Wilcoxon signed-rank test for H0: zero median effect, p=0.021).
evidence: This is a summary of the DDM parameter fitting results with statistical test.

claim: Consistent with model predictions from Ratcliff and Frank, 2012, and Wei et al., 2015, microstimulation affected parameters that controlled the decision bound (a, B_collapse, B_t) in 16 sessions each.
source: Consistent with model predictions from Ratcliff and Frank, 2012, and Wei et al., 2015, microstimulation affected parameters that controlled the decision bound (a, B_collapse, B_t) in 16 sessions each (not necessarily in the same sessions for each parameter, see Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a summary of the DDM parameter fitting results related to specific theoretical predictions.

claim: The changes in the maximal decision bound (a) were variable across sessions (p=0.68).
source: The changes in the maximal decision bound (a) were variable across sessions (p=0.68).
evidence: This is a summary of the DDM parameter fitting results with statistical test.

claim: The changes in the collapsing bound dynamics (B_collapse, B_t) tended to indicate faster and earlier decreases in bounds (p=0.039 and 0.088, respectively).
source: The changes in the collapsing bound dynamics (B_collapse, B_t) tended to indicate faster and earlier decreases in bounds (p=0.039 and 0.088, respectively).
evidence: This is a summary of the DDM parameter fitting results with statistical tests.

claim: Consistent with model predictions from Ratcliff and Frank, 2012, microstimulation caused changes in non-decision times in 30 sessions (t0_Contra and t0_Ipsi).
source: Consistent with model predictions from Ratcliff and Frank, 2012, microstimulation caused changes in non-decision times in 30 sessions (t0_Contra and t0_Ipsi).
evidence: This is a summary of the DDM parameter fitting results related to a specific theoretical prediction.

claim: The changes in non-decision times varied from session to session (p=0.28 and 0.75, respectively).
source: These changes varied from session to session (p=0.28 and 0.75, respectively).
evidence: This is a summary of the DDM parameter fitting results with statistical tests.

claim: STN microstimulation induced offsets in momentary (me; n=16 sessions; p=0.61) and accumulated (z; n=12 sessions; p=0.016) evidence.
source: First, consistent with the above-demonstrated microstimulation-induced choice biases (Figure 5), microstimulation induced offsets in momentary (me; n=16 sessions; p=0.61) and accumulated (z; n=12 sessions; p=0.016) evidence.
evidence: This is a summary of the DDM parameter fitting results with statistical tests.

claim: The microstimulation effects involved changes in more than one model parameter in the majority of sessions.
source: Second, the microstimulation effects involved changes in more than one model parameter in the majority of sessions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a summary of the DDM parameter fitting results shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The STN is causally involved in multiple decision-related functions, including those mediating the dependence on evidence, choice biases, and bound dynamics.
source: These results suggest that the STN is causally involved in multiple decision-related functions, including those mediating the dependence on evidence, choice biases, and bound dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the DDM fitting results.

claim: STN neurons with different functional roles are located close to one another.
source: The multi-faceted microstimulation effects, combined with the fact that the kind of microstimulation we used tends to activate not just one neuron, but rather groups of neurons near the tip of the electrode (Tehovnik, 1996), suggested that STN neurons with different functional roles are located close to one another.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the microstimulation effects and known properties of electrical microstimulation.

claim: Neurons that were classified as belonging to different clusters tended to be intermingled.
source: Consistent with this idea, neurons that were classified as belonging to different clusters tended to be intermingled (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a description of the spatial distribution of neurons shown in Figure 7.

claim: No consistent topographical organization patterns were observed within or between the two monkeys.
source: We did not observe any consistent topographical organization patterns within or between the two monkeys.
evidence: This is a summary of the spatial analysis of neuron locations.

claim: At certain locations, neurons belonging to different clusters were recorded using the same electrode.
source: At certain locations, neurons belonging to different clusters were recorded using the same electrode.
evidence: This is a description of the spatial distribution of neurons.

claim: The mean silhouette scores for spatial clustering were –0.09 and –0.11 for the two monkeys, respectively, indicating that neurons were often closer to others from a different cluster than those within the same cluster.
source: We calculated silhouette scores to quantify whether the activity pattern-based neuron clusters also formed clusters in the 3D physical space. The mean values were –0.09 and –0.11 for the two monkeys, respectively, indicating that neurons were often closer to others from a different cluster than those within the same cluster.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the spatial distribution of neurons.

claim: STN subpopulations did not segregate from each other and instead tended to be intermingled.
source: In other words, STN subpopulations did not segregate from each other and instead tended to be intermingled, and thus microstimulation likely activated multiple neurons with different functional properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial analysis of neuron locations.

claim: Microstimulation likely activated multiple neurons with different functional properties.
source: In other words, STN subpopulations did not segregate from each other and instead tended to be intermingled, and thus microstimulation likely activated multiple neurons with different functional properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the intermingled spatial distribution of neurons.

claim: The second cluster was associated with lower overall likelihood of observing microstimulation effects compared to other clusters (Chi-square test, H0: the likelihood is the same for the first cluster and the other clusters; p=0.003).
source: We found that the second cluster was associated with lower overall likelihood of observing microstimulation effects compared to other clusters (Figure 8B; Chi-square test, H0: the likelihood is the same for the first cluster and the other clusters; p=0.003), while the third cluster had higher overall likelihood (p=0.035).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the relationship between neuron clusters and microstimulation effects.

claim: The third cluster had higher overall likelihood of observing microstimulation effects (p=0.035).
source: We found that the second cluster was associated with lower overall likelihood of observing microstimulation effects compared to other clusters (Figure 8B; Chi-square test, H0: the likelihood is the same for the first cluster and the other clusters; p=0.003), while the third cluster had higher overall likelihood (p=0.035).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the relationship between neuron clusters and microstimulation effects.

claim: For the first three clusters, no microstimulation effect dominated (p>0.3 for all).
source: For the first three clusters, no microstimulation effect dominated (p>0.3 for all), whereas for the fourth cluster, it was more likely to observe effects on non-decision times (i.e. with neural activity patterns not related to the three models; p=0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the relationship between neuron clusters and specific microstimulation effects.

claim: For the fourth cluster, it was more likely to observe effects on non-decision times (i.e. with neural activity patterns not related to the three models; p=0.001).
